explanations.answer: God is with him in all he does
explanations.explanation: That's exactly what Abimelech says: "God is with you in all that you do." (Genesis 21:22) Abimelech, king of Gerar (Genesis 20:2), says it together with Phicol, the commander of his army. They could have opened with anything. They led with God. Nobody is complimenting Abraham's cookie recipe here, friend.

explanations.answer: His flocks grow bigger every year
explanations.explanation: Good guess, because flocks matter in this story. But the text doesn't have Abimelech say a word about flocks. He says, "God is with you in all that you do." (Genesis 21:22) Abraham's sheep show up later, when he gives some to Abimelech (Genesis 21:27).

Ooh, a little power-bragging, I see where you were going. But Abimelech never counts servants in this passage. He says, "God is with you in all that you do." (Genesis 21:22) That line is about God, not about headcount, friend.

Yes, that's the word. Abimelech asks Abraham to swear that he will not "deal falsely" with him or his children or descendants. (Genesis 21:23) He wants honesty to last past his own lifetime. I think that's a king who plans ahead, because I can't even plan past lunch.

Harshly sounds close, but it's not the word. Abimelech asks Abraham to swear that he will not "deal falsely" with him or his children or descendants. (Genesis 21:23) The oath is about dealing honestly, not about being rough. Good guess, though, friend.

Proudly is a fun one, but no. The oath is about being straight with people. Abimelech asks that Abraham not "deal falsely" with him or his children or descendants. (Genesis 21:23) Pride never comes up.
True! Abraham answers, "I swear it." (Genesis 21:24) That's all he says. Three words, and the oath is agreed. I wish my answers to "what do you want for dinner" were that short.
Actually, it's true. Abraham agrees to the oath, and he answers, "I swear it." (Genesis 21:24) He doesn't turn Abimelech down at all. Stick with me, friend, you'll catch the next one.

explanations.answer: A well the king's servants seized
explanations.explanation: That's it. Abraham complained to Abimelech "…about a well that Abimelech’s servants had seized…" (Genesis 21:25) The servants took the well, and Abraham brought his complaint to the king. Picture someone eating the last cookie you were saving, and you're the one walking up to the boss about it. Abraham just took it straight to the top.

explanations.answer: Sheep stolen out of his flock
explanations.explanation: Not sheep this time. The complaint was about a well that Abimelech's servants had seized. (Genesis 21:25) Sheep do show up in the story, but they come as Abraham's gift (Genesis 21:27). Nobody's stealing from the flock here.

explanations.answer: A field the king's army burned
explanations.explanation: That would be quite a complaint, friend, but it's not in the text. Abraham complained about a well that Abimelech's servants had seized. (Genesis 21:25) No fire and no burned field. Just a well, and a complaint brought to the king.

Right. Abimelech says, "I do not know who has done this. You did not tell me, so I have not heard about it until today." (Genesis 21:26) Notice he says two things: he doesn't know who did it, and Abraham hadn't told him. That's a lot of "I don't know" packed into one answer.

This one's actually true. Abimelech says, "I do not know who has done this. You did not tell me, so I have not heard about it until today." (Genesis 21:26) He says he's hearing about the well for the first time. He doesn't say he knew all along.

Yes! Abraham gave Abimelech sheep and cattle, "…and the two men made a covenant." (Genesis 21:27) A covenant is a solemn agreement between two parties. The text puts the gift and the covenant side by side in one verse. I'd say that beats a handshake and a smile.
A feast would be nice, and I'm not against one. But the text says the two men made a covenant. (Genesis 21:27) The sheep and cattle were a gift to Abimelech, not a menu.

I see why animals made you think of sacrifice. But the text says Abraham gave the sheep and cattle to Abimelech, "…and the two men made a covenant." (Genesis 21:27) The animals went to the king, so this one's not a sacrifice.

explanations.answer: His witness that he dug the well
explanations.explanation: Exactly. Abraham says, "You are to accept the seven ewe lambs from my hand as my witness that I dug this well." (Genesis 21:30) Seven lambs, and every one of them is a witness. Abimelech asked a simple question and got a simple answer. I've had cookie orders with less paperwork than this well.

explanations.answer: A gift for the king's children
explanations.explanation: That's a kind guess, but Abraham doesn't say a word about the king's children when he explains the lambs. He says, "You are to accept the seven ewe lambs from my hand as my witness that I dug this well." (Genesis 21:30) They're a witness, not a present for the kids.

explanations.answer: An offering for a safe journey
explanations.explanation: Nope, no trip is mentioned here. Abraham tells Abimelech, "You are to accept the seven ewe lambs from my hand as my witness that I dug this well." (Genesis 21:30) The lambs are about the well, friend.

Yes, Beersheba. The text says the place "…was called Beersheba, because it was there that the two of them swore an oath." (Genesis 21:31) The name comes from what happened right on that spot. It's like a bakery named after the first batch that ever came out of its oven. You hear the name, and you know the story.

Bethel is a place in Abraham's story, but it's not this one. Genesis 12:8 mentions it earlier, when Abram pitches his tent with Bethel on the west. The place where the two men swore their oath "…was called Beersheba…" (Genesis 21:31) Close, but Bethel will have to wait.

Hebron comes up in Abraham's story too. Genesis 13:18 says he settled by the oaks of Mamre at Hebron. But it's not the answer here. The text says the place where the two swore an oath "…was called Beersheba…" (Genesis 21:31) You're thinking along the right trail, friend.

True. "After they had made the covenant at Beersheba, Abimelech and Phicol the commander of his army got up and returned to the land of the Philistines." (Genesis 21:32) The covenant comes first, and then they go. The very next verse has Abraham planting a tamarisk tree at Beersheba. (Genesis 21:33) So the story keeps going, friend.
Actually, it's true. The text says Abimelech and Phicol "…got up and returned to the land of the Philistines." (Genesis 21:32) They don't stay at Beersheba after the covenant.

explanations.answer: He calls on the name of the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's right. At Beersheba, Abraham planted a tamarisk tree, "…and there he called upon the name of the LORD, the Eternal God." (Genesis 21:33) He plants, and then he prays. I think that's a good order for any day.

explanations.answer: He builds a house for Sarah
explanations.explanation: Sarah is Abraham's wife (Genesis 17:15), so I see why she came to mind. But the text never says Abraham builds a house for her here. It says he planted a tamarisk tree, "…and there he called upon the name of the LORD, the Eternal God." (Genesis 21:33) The tree and the prayer are what happen at Beersheba.

explanations.answer: He digs a second well nearby
explanations.explanation: Another well is a fair guess, since a well is what this whole passage keeps coming back to. But the text doesn't say that. It says Abraham planted a tamarisk tree, "…and there he called upon the name of the LORD, the Eternal God." (Genesis 21:33) No new well is mentioned, friend.
Not quite, friend. The text says, "…Abraham resided in the land of the Philistines for a long time." (Genesis 21:34) A long time isn't "soon." He stays put for a good while.
Right, it's false. The text says, "…Abraham resided in the land of the Philistines for a long time." (Genesis 21:34) He's not rushing off, and he settles in for a long stay.
